Jonah 1.summary: The LORD tells Jonah son of Amittai to go to Nineveh and cry out against its wickedness (Jonah 1:1–2). Instead Jonah heads to Joppa and boards a ship bound for Tarshish, seeking to flee from the LORD's presence (Jonah 1:3). A violent storm threatens the vessel. The frightened sailors pray to their own gods and throw cargo overboard, while Jonah sleeps below deck (Jonah 1:4–6). After lots identify Jonah, he tells the crew he worships the LORD, maker of sea and land, and admits he is fleeing from God (Jonah 1:7–10). He proposes that they throw him into the sea; they first try to row ashore but cannot, then pray that they not be held guilty before casting him overboard (Jonah 1:11–15). The sea becomes calm, and the sailors fear the LORD, offering a sacrifice and making vows (Jonah 1:15–16). The LORD appoints a great fish to swallow Jonah, who remains in it three days and nights (Jonah 1:17). The chapter contrasts Jonah's flight with the sailors' growing reverence and highlights divine authority over sea, storm, and Jonah's mission. The account calls the creature a "great fish"; it does not identify its species.
Jonah 1.whereWeAre: Obadiah closed with the promise that "the kingdom shall be the LORD's," after judging Edom for betraying Judah (Obadiah 1:21). Jonah opens the next book with an entirely different test of that kingship: God sends a prophet to warn a hostile foreign city, Nineveh, and Jonah flees in the opposite direction instead, triggering a storm that terrifies the pagan sailors around him. Thrown overboard and swallowed by a great fish, Jonah's flight ends in chapter 2, where he prays for rescue from the one place left to run.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Divine speaker and actor. Commands Jonah, sends the storm, and appoints the fish (1:1–4,17)

keyFigures.name: Jonah son of Amittai
keyFigures.role: Israelite messenger who flees his commission. His resistance sets the voyage and crisis in motion; he identifies the LORD as Creator (1:1–3,9–12)

keyFigures.name: The sailors and shipmaster
keyFigures.role: Non-Israelite crew and captain. Pray, seek to preserve life, and come to fear the LORD (1:5–16)

keyFigures.name: The great fish
keyFigures.role: Creature appointed by God in the narrative. Swallows Jonah after he is cast into the sea (1:17)

keyFigures.name: The people of Nineveh
keyFigures.role: Intended recipients of Jonah’s mission, not present in the scene. Their wickedness is named as the reason for the commission (1:2)

keyThemes.explanation: Jonah is told to preach against Nineveh's wickedness but instead books passage in the opposite direction, showing that even a called prophet can choose flight over obedience (1:1-3).
The LORD controls the storm that nearly destroys the ship and later appoints a great fish to save Jonah, showing power over both sea and creature (1:4, 1:9, 1:17).
The sailors try rowing to shore before throwing Jonah overboard, and pray not to be held guilty for his death, showing a reluctance to take a life even to save their own (1:11-15).

keyThemes.theme: Recognition of the LORD among outsiders
keyThemes.explanation: The pagan sailors move from praying to their own gods, to urging Jonah to call on his God, to fearing the LORD directly and offering sacrifice once the sea calms (1:5-6, 1:14-16).

Jonah 2.summary: From inside the fish Jonah prays to the LORD (Jonah 2:1). His poem remembers an overwhelming experience of waters, depths, and waves, when he felt driven from God's sight yet still looked toward God's holy temple (Jonah 2:2–4). Water closes over him, seaweed wraps around his head, and he describes descending to the roots of the mountains and the land of bars before the LORD brings his life up from the pit (Jonah 2:5–6). In his distress he remembers the LORD, and his prayer reaches God's holy temple (Jonah 2:7). He contrasts those who cling to empty idols with his own promise to sacrifice with thanksgiving and fulfill his vows, declaring that salvation belongs to the LORD (Jonah 2:8–9). At God's command the fish releases Jonah onto dry land (Jonah 2:10). The chapter is a thanksgiving prayer for rescue from drowning, even though Jonah's wider assignment remains unfinished. Its language is poetic, picturing Jonah's rescue through images of drowning and the underworld rather than a literal geographical journey.
Jonah 2.whereWeAre: Chapter 1 ended with Jonah thrown into the sea and swallowed by a great fish the LORD had appointed (Jonah 1:17). Chapter 2 pauses the action for Jonah's prayer from inside the fish, a thanksgiving psalm that moves from vivid images of drowning and despair to a renewed hope that salvation belongs to the LORD. That rescue, when the fish releases Jonah onto dry land, sets up chapter 3, where Jonah finally receives his original commission to Nineveh a second time.

keyFigures.name: Jonah
keyFigures.role: Speaker of the thanksgiving prayer. Recalls his danger, appeals to God, and makes vows of thanks (2:1–9)

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Recipient of prayer and agent of deliverance. Hears Jonah and commands the fish to release him (2:2,6–7,10)

keyFigures.name: The great fish
keyFigures.role: Creature sheltering Jonah according to the story. Provides the setting for the prayer and ejects him at God’s command (2:1,10)

keyFigures.name: Those who regard lying vanities
keyFigures.role: Contrasting group invoked in Jonah's poetry as those who cling to worthless idols. Their misplaced loyalties are contrasted with Jonah's thanksgiving (2:8); no individuals are named

keyThemes.explanation: From inside the fish, with no other hope of rescue, Jonah turns to prayer, describing his situation in the vivid language of drowning and abandonment (2:1-4).
Even as he sinks toward the roots of the mountains, Jonah says that remembering the LORD is what brings his prayer to God's holy temple (2:5-7).
Jonah credits the LORD alone with bringing his life up from the pit and commanding the fish to release him, crediting no other power for his rescue (2:6, 2:9-10).
Jonah contrasts those who cling to worthless idols with his own promise to sacrifice and fulfill his vows, turning his rescue into an occasion for gratitude (2:8-9).

Jonah 3.summary: The word of the LORD comes to Jonah a second time with the command to go to Nineveh and proclaim the message given to him (Jonah 3:1–2). This time Jonah goes. The narrator describes Nineveh as an exceedingly great city, associated with a three-days' journey, but does not define the precise measurement (Jonah 3:3). Jonah enters the city and warns, "Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown" (Jonah 3:4). The people believe God, announce a fast, and wear sackcloth from the greatest to the least (Jonah 3:5). News reaches the king of Nineveh, who leaves his throne, sets aside his robe, puts on sackcloth, and sits in ashes (Jonah 3:6). A royal proclamation calls people to fast, including livestock, to cry urgently to God, and to turn from evil and violence (Jonah 3:7–9). The king expresses hope, not certainty, that God may turn from judgment. God sees their turning from evil and does not bring the announced calamity upon the city (Jonah 3:10). The chapter emphasizes that response to warning involves changed conduct, especially ending violence, and portrays judgment as averted by repentance rather than by status or ritual alone.
Jonah 3.whereWeAre: Chapter 2 ended with the fish releasing Jonah safely onto dry land after his prayer of thanksgiving (Jonah 2:10). Chapter 3 gives Jonah a second chance: this time he goes to Nineveh, and the entire city, from the king down to the animals, responds to his warning with fasting and genuine repentance. Because God relents from the announced judgment, chapter 4 turns from the city's response to Jonah's own reaction, anger instead of relief, at the mercy he predicted God would show.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Speaker and judge. Renews the commission and responds to the city's turning from evil (3:1–2,10)

keyFigures.name: Jonah
keyFigures.role: Prophetic messenger. Obeys the renewed command and announces impending judgment (3:3–4)

keyFigures.name: The people of Nineveh
keyFigures.role: Hearers of the warning. Believe God, fast, put on sackcloth, and turn from evil (3:5,8–10)

keyFigures.name: The king of Nineveh
keyFigures.role: Unnamed ruler in the account. Models humility and authorizes a proclamation urging repentance (3:6–9)

keyFigures.name: The king’s nobles
keyFigures.role: Officials named alongside the king. Join in issuing the decree (3:7)

keyFigures.name: Animals of the city
keyFigures.role: Livestock included in the decree. The narrative explicitly extends fasting and sackcloth measures to animals (3:7–8)

keyThemes.explanation: God gives Jonah the same commission a second time, and this time Jonah actually goes to Nineveh and delivers the warning (3:1-4).
Jonah's blunt forty-day warning is not the end of the story; the Ninevites respond immediately with belief, fasting, and sackcloth rather than despair (3:4-5).
The king's decree does not stop at religious ritual; it specifically calls the people to turn from evil and violence, showing repentance meant as a change in behavior, not only in feeling (3:7-10).

keyThemes.theme: Mercy in the face of judgment
keyThemes.explanation: Because the city turns from its evil way, God relents from the disaster he had announced, showing judgment as conditional on response rather than fixed in advance (3:9-10).

Jonah 4.summary: Jonah is deeply displeased and angry because God did not destroy Nineveh (Jonah 4:1). He prays that this is why he fled toward Tarshish: he knew the LORD to be gracious, merciful, slow to anger, abundant in kindness, and willing to turn from announced calamity (Jonah 4:2). Jonah asks to die rather than live, and God asks whether his anger is right (Jonah 4:3–4). Jonah goes east of the city, builds a shelter, and watches to see what will happen (Jonah 4:5). God appoints a plant to give shade, bringing Jonah great relief; then God appoints a worm to damage the plant and a scorching east wind, leaving Jonah faint and again wishing to die (Jonah 4:6–8). When God asks whether Jonah is right to be angry about the plant, Jonah insists he is (Jonah 4:9). God contrasts Jonah’s concern for a plant he did not cultivate with divine concern for Nineveh, home to more than 120,000 people who do not know their right hand from their left, and much livestock (Jonah 4:10–11). The book ends with God’s unanswered question, challenging the reader to consider compassion for those Jonah regards with resentment. The right-hand/left-hand phrase likely points to moral innocence, perhaps young children too immature to know right from wrong, though readers differ on exactly how the number 120,000 should be understood.
Jonah 4.whereWeAre: Chapter 3 ended with Nineveh's repentance and God relenting from the disaster Jonah had announced (Jonah 3:10). Chapter 4 reveals why Jonah fled in the first place: he resents the LORD's mercy toward Israel's enemy and would rather die than watch Nineveh spared. The book closes on God's own unanswered question about compassion for a great city, leaving readers, not just Jonah, to weigh the same choice before Micah, the next book, turns from mercy for outsiders back to judgment on Israel and Judah's own corrupt leaders.

keyFigures.name: Jonah
keyFigures.role: Displeased messenger. Objects to God’s mercy, shelters outside Nineveh, and grieves the plant (4:1–9)

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Questioner and compassionate divine actor. Provides and removes shade and asks why Nineveh should not be spared (4:4,6–11)

keyFigures.name: The people of Nineveh
keyFigures.role: Recipients of divine concern, referred to in dialogue. The city’s many inhabitants are contrasted with Jonah’s concern for the plant (4:11)

keyFigures.name: The plant, worm, and east wind
keyFigures.role: Created agents used in the narrative. Provide comfort and then distress through which Jonah is challenged (4:6–8)

keyFigures.name: The livestock of Nineveh
keyFigures.role: Animals explicitly included in God's closing question. Emphasize the breadth of divine concern in the narrative (4:11)

keyThemes.explanation: Jonah is angrier about Nineveh being spared than he ever was about his own danger, revealing that his real objection was always to God's mercy toward this enemy city (4:1-4).
Jonah mourns the loss of a plant that gave him one day of shade far more than he ever grieved for Nineveh's hundreds of thousands of people (4:5-9).
God's closing argument contrasts Jonah's concern for a plant he did not grow with God's own concern for a great city full of people and animals Jonah never had to care for (4:10-11).
The book ends with God's question left hanging, unanswered by Jonah or any narrated outcome, inviting every later reader to supply their own answer (4:9-11).
